Cell groups and latent factors

This tutorial covers the core steps of CellTFusion: building cell groups from TF modules and deconvolution features, extracting latent factors and characterizing cell niches. It uses two objects from the Feature computation tutorial:

  • network — TF co-activity modules from compute.WTCNA().
  • dt — deconvolution subgroups from multideconv::compute.deconvolution.analysis().

Cell groups

construct_cell_groups() correlates each TF module with the deconvolution features, clusters the significantly correlated features of each module, and cuts the dendrograms into cell groups. Features are clustered on the value of their correlation with the module, so a cell group is a set of features with a similar biological activity: features related to the same TF module to the same degree, which do not need to vary together across samples. Each cell group covers a single range of correlation values: the dendrogram is cut with a dynamic tree cut, clusters made of separated ranges are split, and pieces smaller than min_cluster_size are joined to the neighbouring group with the closest correlation. Each cell group gets a composite score per sample: the first canonical component of a canonical correlation analysis (CCA) between the group’s deconvolution features and the score of its TF module, i.e. the combination of the features that correlates most with the module score. The score is oriented to be aligned with the TF module: a positive score means that the sample is on the active side of the module for that cell group, a negative score that it is on the inactive side.

Key arguments:

  • network, dt — the inputs above.
  • batch — optional cohort vector (see Multi-cohort analysis).
  • pval — p-value threshold to select the deconvolution features significantly correlated with each module.
  • file_name / return — with return = TRUE (default), the colored dendrograms are saved to Results/Dendrogram_color_clusters_<file_name>.pdf, and the composition and the scores of the cell groups to Results/Cell.groups.composition_<file_name>.csv and Results/Cell.groups.scores_<file_name>.csv.
cell_groups <- construct_cell_groups(
  network           = network,
  dt                = dt,
  pval              = 0.05,
  clustering_method = "ward.D2",
  file_name         = "Tutorial"
)

One dendrogram is drawn per TF module, showing how its correlated deconvolution features cluster into cell groups. The leaves are drawn in the order of their correlation with the module as far as the tree allows, and the groups are numbered from the lowest to the highest correlation. The number written next to each group is the one in the cell group name (Dendrogram_<module>_group_<number>); a group that the tree splits into two places is drawn, and numbered, in both. Features that are not assigned to any cluster are not part of any cell group:

construct_cell_groups() returns a named list:

Element Description
Cell_groups Data frame of composite scores (samples x cell groups)
Composition Deconvolution features in each cell group
Weights CCA projection parameters of each group (xcoef, train_means, train_sds; only xcoef with batch), used to score new samples

Re-running with precomputed features

CellTFusion() accepts precomputed dt, tfs and pathways, for example from a previous run (res$Processed_deconvolution, res$TFs_matrix, res$Pathways_scores). The corresponding steps are then skipped, which is useful to try different module or cell group parameters without recomputing the features:

res_rerun <- CellTFusion(
  raw_counts = raw.counts,
  normalized = TRUE,
  dt         = res$Processed_deconvolution,
  tfs        = res$TFs_matrix,
  pathways   = res$Pathways_scores,
  corr_mod   = 0.8,    # e.g. merge modules more readily than the default 0.9
  min_module_size     = 10,
  pval       = 0.05,
  return     = TRUE
)

Latent factors

compute.latent_factors() decomposes the cell group scores into non-negative latent factors with NMF. Only the positive part of each score is used, max(score, 0): how far the sample is on the active side of the group’s TF module (negative scores become 0), so the factors describe the high-activity direction of the cell groups. If rank = NULL, the number of factors is chosen among ranks (2 to 15 by default, never more than the number of cell groups) with bootstrap NMF: for each rank, NMF is fitted on all the patients and on n_boot (100) bootstrap samples of the patients, and the factors of each run are matched to the reference factors by the cosine similarity of their profiles (their weights on the cell groups). Each factor gets its recovery frequency (proportion of runs in which it is found, similarity >= similarity_thresh) and its mean similarity; a factor is robust when both pass the thresholds (recovery_thresh = 0.7 and similarity_thresh = 0.8 by default, starting points rather than universal cutoffs). Two factors of the same rank with very similar profiles are flagged as redundant. The selected rank is the largest one whose factors are all robust and none redundant: as many factors as the data support reliably (low ranks capture the dominant patterns and are almost always stable, so the smallest stable rank would favour 2). rank_selection reports every candidate rank and stability the factors of the selected one; when two adjacent ranks are similarly good, check whether the main factors persist at the neighbouring rank.

latent_spaces <- compute.latent_factors(
  scores    = cell_groups$Cell_groups,
  rank      = NULL,
  seed      = 123,
  file_name = "Tutorial",
  return    = TRUE
)

head(latent_spaces$Z)          # samples x factors
latent_spaces$rank_selection   # stability and redundancy of each candidate rank
latent_spaces$stability        # recovery and mean similarity of each factor

With return = TRUE, the stability of each candidate rank is plotted (Results/NMF_rank_stability_<file_name>.pdf, followed by a page with the recovery and mean similarity of each factor of the selected rank). On the tutorial data, ranks 2 to 5 have all their factors robust and none redundant, and stability drops from rank 6, so 5 factors are kept:

The result contains Z (factor scores, samples x factors — the input for statistics), W (weights of each cell group in each factor), nmf_input (the positive part of the scores), the NMF model, the per-sample factor proportions and the stability tables. The NMF approximates the transposed input as W %*% diag(d) %*% t(Z): each column of W and each column of Z sums to 1, and the size of each factor is in nmf_model$d. Tests on one factor at a time do not depend on this scaling; the factor proportions of each sample (Z multiplied by d, divided by its sum per sample) take the sizes into account. project_factors() projects the cell group scores of new samples (from compute.test.set()) onto the factors, on the scale of Z. With return = TRUE, the mixture of factors in each sample is plotted:

Cell niches

compute_cells_niches() characterizes each latent factor by the cell groups that contribute most to it: the top_n cell groups with the highest weight in the factor (W), described by their deconvolution features and the CCA coefficients of these features in the cell group scores. The deconvolution features are kept as they are (subgroups are not expanded into their members).

cells_niches <- compute_cells_niches(
  latent_factors = latent_spaces,
  cell_groups    = cell_groups,
  top_n          = 5,
  return         = TRUE,
  file_name      = "Tutorial"
)

The result has one row per factor, cell group and feature (factor, cell_group, module, weight, feature, coefficient). For each factor, a tree network is saved (one page per factor): the factor on the left, its top cell groups in the middle (coloured by their TF module) and their features listed on the right. Edges are the CCA coefficients: red when the feature is higher in samples where the cell group is active, blue when it is lower; coefficients close to zero are thin. Features correlated with each other (e.g. several estimates of the same cell type) share their weight, so a single small edge with the opposite colour of its cell group should be read together with the rest of the group.

A heatmap shows the NMF weights of all the cell groups in all factors (cell groups ordered by the factor where their weight is highest; outlined: the top cell groups of each factor), so that cell groups shared between factors can be seen:
